concept.name: Price-to-sales ratio
concept.definition: Market capitalization divided by trailing revenue - equivalently price per share over revenue per share - the amount investors pay per dollar of a company's sales. It remains usable when earnings are negative, which the P/E ratio is not.
concept.intuition: Sales are the hardest income-statement line to fake and exist even for loss-making firms, so P/S is the multiple of last resort for young or distressed companies.
concept.mechanics: Divide market capitalization by trailing-twelve-month revenue. Because the ratio ignores costs entirely, it must be read alongside margins: a firm at 1x sales with 20% net margins is effectively on a 5x P/E.
concept.formula: P/S = Market capitalization / Trailing 12-month revenue = Price per share / Revenue per share.
concept.failure_modes: It treats a dollar of grocery revenue like a dollar of software revenue, so low-margin, high-revenue firms look deceptively cheap, and it ignores leverage - EV/Sales is the better tool for indebted firms.
concept.misconceptions: A low P/S does not imply undervaluation - thin-margin businesses rationally trade near zero - and the ratio says nothing about whether sales will ever convert to profit.
concept.example: A retailer with a $50 billion market cap and $100 billion of sales trades at 0.5x sales; with a 2% net margin that equates to a P/E of 25 - not obviously a bargain.

citations.source: Aswath Damodaran (NYU Stern), Relative Valuation lecture notes (Packet 2)
citations.section: Multiples are standardized estimates of price
